The solutions are exactly the functions $f(x)=c\max\{0,-x\}$ for an arbitrary constant $c\ge 0$, i.e.
$$\boxed{f(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\ge 0\\ -cx,&x<0\end{cases}\qquad (c\ge 0)}$$

**Derivation.** Let $P(x,y)$ be the assertion and $c=f(0)$. From $P(0,y)$ we get $f(f(y))=c(y-2)$. If $c\neq0$, then $f$ is bijective; putting $y=0$ gives $f(x^2)=c|x|-c-f(c)$. Surjectivity lets us solve $f(y)=x^2$, yielding $f(2+|x|+k/c)=x^2$ for a constant $k$, so $f$ is eventually quadratic on $[2+k/c,\infty)$ while $f(x^2)$ forces it to be $c\sqrt{x}+k$ on $[0,\infty)$ — incompatible growth. Hence $c=0$, so $f(0)=0$ and $f(f(y))\equiv0$.

Now $P(x,0)$ gives $f(x^2)=0$, so $f(t)=0$ for all $t\ge0$. With $P(-1,y)$ we obtain $f(-y)=f(y)+ay$ where $a=f(-1)$; for $y>0$ this gives $f(-y)=ay$, i.e. $f(x)=-ax$ for $x<0$. The condition $f(f(y))=0$ forces $f(y)\ge0$ for $y<0$, hence $a\ge0$. Direct substitution verifies every such function satisfies the original equation (since $f(x^2)=f(f(y))=0$ and $|x|f(y)+yf(x)=f(xy)$ holds case-by-case).
